The great success of MLLM is inseparable from its compositional training paradigm, which independently pre-trains visual encoders [28] and LLMs [61], and then integrates them through additional multimodal training. Due to the engineering simplicity and effectiveness, this paradigm has dominated MLLM area over the past few years. However, the shortcomings of compositional training have been gradually recognized by the community recently, e.g., unclear multimodal scaling property [19, 56]. Therefore, increasing attention has been directed toward the development of more native MLLMs. As illustrated in Fig. 1, native MLLMs aim to jointly optimize both visual and language spaces in an end-to-end manner, thereby maximizing vision-language alignment. Compared to the compositional paradigm, existing native MLLM methods demonstrate a promising scaling law and a significantly simplified training process [9, 56]. Despite these advancements, the primary benefits of native MLLMs are often evaluated under the assumption of infinite training resources, overlooking the substantial challenges posed by limited data and large-scale training. Consequently, a critical practical question remains: whether and how native MLLMs can feasibly achieve or even surpass the performance upper bound of top-tier MLLMs at an acceptable cost. Figure 1: Comparison of design choices, scaling properties, and performance of our native MLLMs. We systematically investigate the designs and the scaling properties of native MLLMs under data constraints and yield valuable findings for building native MLLMs. After adopting these findings, our native MLLMs achieve competitive performance with top-tier MLLMs. \\mathcal { V } _ { d , w } ^ { * } ( \\cdot ) denotes the visual encoder with optimal parameter size. To answer this question, in this paper, we aim to systematically investigate the designs and the scaling properties of native MLLMs under data constraint. Specifically, we first explore the choices of key components in the native architecture including the mixture-of-experts, the visual encoder and the initialization of the LLM. Our findings can be summarized in two folds. Firstly, an appropriate pre-training initialization (e.g., the base LLM) of the LLM greatly benefits the training convergence on multimodal data. Secondly, combining visual encoder architectures and MoEs results in obvious gains against the vanilla decoder-only LLM. Following these findings, we build a meta architecture that optimally balances performance and training cost. Based on the optimal meta architecture, we further explore the scaling properties of the visual encoder, the LLM and the entire native MLLM. Specifically, we first scale up the LLM and the visual encoder independently and observe different scaling properties: while scaling LLM exhibits similar patterns as the conventional language scaling laws, scaling visual encoder shows an upper bound in return due to the limitation of the LLM’s capacity, suggesting that the optimal encoder size varies with the LLM size. Further analysis reveals that the optimal encoder size increases approximately proportionally with the LLM size in log scale. This observation yields a different guidance against compositional paradigm, which employs a visual encoder of one size across all LLM scales. Based on above principles, we propose a native MLLM called NaViL, combined with a simple and cost-effective recipe. To validate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks to evaluate its multimodal capabilities including image captioning [10, 67, 2], optical character recognition (OCR) [57, 17, 39], etc. Experimental results reveal that with { \\sim } 6 0 0 \\mathbf { M } pretraining image-text pairs, NaViL achieves competitive performance compared to current top-tier compositional MLLMs, highlighting the great practicality and capabilities of NaViL. In summary, our contributions are as follows: • We systematically explore the design space and the optimal choice in native MLLMs under data constraint, including the LLM initialization, the visual encoder and the MoEs, and draw three critical findings that greatly benefit the training of native MLLMs. • Based on above findings, we construct a novel native MLLM called NaViL. In NaViL, we explore the scaling properties of the visual encoder and the LLM and indicate their positively correlated scaling relationship. • We conduct large-scale pre-training and fine-tuning experiments on NaViL. Experimental results show that NaViL can achieve top-tier performance with nearly 600M pre-training data. Alternatively, initializing the model from a pre-trained LLM effectively leverages linguistic prior knowledge, significantly reducing data and computational demands. Fig. 10 further illustrates the difference between compositional MLLMs and native MLLMs. Compositional MLLMs typically have different components initialized by separate unimodal pre-training, where different training objectives and strategies are employed to train the LLM and visual encoder. For example, the visual encoder can be trained using an image-text contrastive learning objective (e.g., CLIP [52], SigLIP [72]) or a self-supervised learning objective (e.g., DINOv2 [51]). The complexity of such training process increases the difficulty of scalability. On the other hand, as discussed in [56], native MLLM optimizes both image and text modalities end-to-end using a unified training objective (i.e., next-token prediction (NTP)). This avoids introducing additional bias and significantly simplifies the scaling effort. # C More Related Works Research on Neural Scaling Laws. The foundational work on Neural Scaling Laws began in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) domain, where [29] established predictable power-law relationships demonstrating that performance loss ( L ) scales reliably with model size ( N ) and data size ( D ) , and that larger, decoder-only Transformer models are more compute-efficient. Following works [23] further extended such research to encoder-decoder architectures, observing consistency in scaling exponents on Neural Machine Translation (NMT) tasks. Driven by these successes, in the vision domain, [71] confirmed the applicability of scaling laws to Vision Transformers (ViT), systematically demonstrating continuous performance improvement by scaling both model size (up to 2 billion parameters) and training data. Most recently, these principles have been generalized to Large Multimodal Models, where [1] developed scaling laws that unify the contributions of text, image, and speech modalities by explicitly modeling synergy and competition as an additive term. Furthering this, [56] explored Native Multimodal Models (NMMs) using Mixture of Experts (MoEs), finding an unbalanced scaling law that suggests scaling training tokens ( D ) is more critical than scaling active parameters ( N ) as the compute budget grows. # D Implementation Details The hyperparameters of model architecture for NaViL-2B and NaViL-9B are listed in Tab. 6, while the hyperparameters of training recipe for NaViL-2B and NaViL-9B are provided in Tab. 7 and Tab. 8, respectively. ## Overview of the plan
## Reproduction Plan for NaViL: Native Multimodal Large Language Model

### 1. Objective
Reproduce the entire NaViL framework as described in the paper, including:
- The architectural design space exploration (initialization, MoE, visual encoder dimensions).
- Scaling law experiments for visual encoder and LLM.
- Full training of NaViL-2B and NaViL-9B models and evaluation on all reported multimodal benchmarks.

Because no official code is available, we will implement all components from scratch using a deep learning framework (e.g., PyTorch). This plan provides a step‑by‑step roadmap covering model architecture, data preparation, training stages, hyperparameters, and evaluation metrics.

### 2. Overall Model Architecture
NaViL follows a **native MLLM** paradigm: a visual encoder, a modality‑aware Mixture‑of‑Experts (MoE) extended LLM, and a connector (downsampling + MLP projection) that maps image features into the LLM’s token space.

#### 2.1 Meta Architecture Components
1. **Visual Encoder** \( \mathcal{V}_{d,w} \):
   - A stack of \( d \) transformer layers with hidden dimension \( w \).
   - Bidirectional attention (non‑causal) with 2D‑RoPE (relative position embeddings for 2D).
   - Patch Embedding layer: divides the image into patches of size \( 16 \times 16 \) (stride=16), then projects to dimension \( w \).
   - Supports arbitrary input resolutions; images are padded to multiples of 32 before patching.

2. **Connector** \( \mathcal{C} \):
   - **Pixel Shuffle**: downsamples the visual token sequence (e.g., reducing spatial dimensions by a factor of 2) to control token count.
   - **MLP Projector**: projects the shuffled feature maps from the encoder’s dimension \( w \) to the LLM’s hidden size.

3. **LLM with Modality‑Specific MoE**:
   - Base LLM: InternLM2‑Base (1.8B) for NaViL‑2B, Qwen3‑8B for NaViL‑9B.
   - Each transformer layer is extended with two experts per modality: one for attention projections (**MHA‑MMoE**) and one for FFN (**FFN‑MMoE**). That is, instead of shared q/k/v/o or FFN weights, each modality has its own set of projection matrices.
   - For each token, based on whether it is a visual token or a linguistic token, the corresponding expert is selected. Only one expert is activated per token (top‑1 gating), so activated parameter count equals the base LLM size plus the visual encoder.
   - Attention calculation remains global and unified: after computing Q, K, V with modality‑specific projections, the same scaled dot‑product attention is applied across all tokens.

   **Formal definition** (as given in the paper):
   - For token \( i \) with modality \( m \in \{\text{visual}, \text{linguistic}\} \) at layer \( l \):
     \[
     \begin{aligned}
     x_{i,m}^{l'} &= x_{i,m}^{l-1} + \text{MHA-MMoE}(\text{RMSNorm}(x_{i,m}^{l-1})) \\
     x_{i,m}^{l}   &= x_{i,m}^{l'} + \text{FFN-MMoE}(\text{RMSNorm}(x_{i,m}^{l'}))
     \end{aligned}
     \]
   - MHA‑MMoE: \( Q, K, V \) computed via \( W_Q^m, W_K^m, W_V^m \); output projection \( W_O^m \).
   - FFN‑MMoE: standard SwiGLU with modality‑specific \( W_{\text{gate}}^m, W_{\text{up}}^m, W_{\text{down}}^m \).

#### 2.2 Special Tokens and Resolution Handling
- `<begin_of_image>`, `<end_of_image>`: wrap each image token subsequence.
- `<end_of_line>`: inserted at the end of every row of image tokens (to preserve 2D positional information).
- **Multi‑scale Packing at Inference**: Given downsampling rate \( \tau = \sqrt{2}/2 \), the input image is repeatedly downsampled until its area falls below a threshold, yielding a multi‑scale pyramid. Each scale is encoded independently by the visual encoder, and all token sequences are concatenated with `<end_of_scale>` between scales. For training, this packing is enabled in most stages (except S1.1 of NaViL-9B for speed).

### 3. Training Pipeline
NaViL is trained in two main stages: **Multi‑modal Generative Pre‑training** (S1) and **Supervised Fine‑tuning** (S2). Pre‑training is further split into S1.1 and S1.2. All stages use **Next‑Token Prediction (NTP)** with an image captioning objective (i.e., the model predicts the next token of the text given preceding visual and textual tokens).

#### 3.1 Data Sources
- **Web‑scale noisy image‑text pairs** (500M): 300M directly from Laion‑2B, Coyo‑700M, Wukong, SA‑1B; 200M generated by captions from InternVL‑8B on these images.
- **High‑quality multimodal alignment data + pure language data** (185M): from InternVL‑2.5 and InternLM2.5, covering captioning, QA, documents, charts, OCR, etc.
- **SFT data** (68M): high‑quality multimodal instructions, also from InternVL‑2.5 suite.

#### 3.2 Stage S1.1 – Generative Pre‑training (vision‑only trainable)
- **Data**: 500M image‑text pairs (described above).
- **Trainable parameters**: Only newly added vision‑specific parameters: visual encoder, MLP projector, and MoE visual experts (the visual expert matrices in attention and FFN). All linguistic parameters (base LLM + MoE linguistic experts) are frozen.
- **Objective**: Next token prediction on concatenated [image tokens, text tokens] sequences.

#### 3.3 Stage S1.2 – High‑quality Alignment (unfreeze attention)

- **Trainable parameters**: The textual parameters inside the self‑attention layers (i.e., the MoE attention modules for linguistic tokens) are unfrozen, while the LLM’s FFN layers remain frozen. Continue training for better cross‑modal integration.

### 5. Model Implementation Details
#### 5.1 Visual Encoder
- Implement a Vision Transformer with bidirectional (non‑causal) self‑attention and 2D Rotary Position Embeddings (e.g., apply RoPE to query/key with spatial position indices).
- Patch embedding: conv2d with kernel 16, stride 16, output channels = \( w \).
- Normalization: RMSNorm.
- Activation: SiLU in FFN (if using SwiGLU) but the paper doesn’t specify details for encoder FFN; we can assume standard SwiGLU similar to LLM.

#### 5.2 Connector
- **Pixel Unshuffle** (pixel shuffle in reverse): reduces spatial resolution by a factor \( r \) (likely 2 or 4) and increases channels. The paper only mentions “downsamples through pixel shuffle” – need to determine exact factor. Based on typical practices (e.g., InternVL), downsampling by 4× (2× in each dimension) is common.
- **MLP Projector**: a 2‑layer MLP with SiLU activation, projecting from encoder output dimension to LLM hidden size.

#### 5.3 Modality‑Specific MoE in LLM
- Base LLM architecture (InternLM2 or Qwen3) must be implemented or loaded from existing checkpoints. Then we extend each transformer layer:
   - Replace the original Q/K/V/O linear layers with a gated module that selects between two sets of weights based on a token’s modality flag.
   - Similarly for the FFN layers (SwiGLU with gate, up, down projections).
- Gating: the modality is known from the token type (derived from the input sequence composition). So we simply route tokens to the corresponding expert matrices; no learned router needed. This keeps inference cost the same as the base LLM (only one expert active per token).
- Attention mask: for images, causal masking is not applied; the full bidirectional attention among image tokens is allowed, while text tokens follow causal masking. However, the paper uses “global attention” across all tokens, meaning visual tokens attend to all other visual and textual tokens, but textual tokens attend only to past textual tokens and all visual tokens. We need to construct a hybrid attention mask accordingly.

#### 5.4 Input Processing
- Image: pad to nearest multiple of 32.
- Apply patch embedding to obtain \( H' \times W' \) visual tokens (\( H' = H/16, W' = W/16 \)).
- Optional multi‑scale: for each scale, resize and encode, then concatenate.
- Insert special tokens: `<begin_of_image>`, `<end_of_image>`, `<end_of_line>` after each row of tokens (requires knowing original spatial arrangement after downsampling). `<end_of_scale>` between scale features.
- Concatenate image tokens with text tokens. Text is tokenized using the LLM’s tokenizer (from InternLM2 or Qwen3). The final sequence length must be ≤ 16384.

- **MoE expert weights initialization**: The new visual expert matrices can be initialized randomly (or copied from the linguistic experts and then fine‑tuned). The paper doesn’t specify – we will initialize randomly with same distribution as LLM.
- **Validation loss computation**: Teacher forcing means the model predicts next token given all preceding tokens (including previous ground truth). For image captioning, the image tokens are provided, and the model predicts the caption tokens.

### 10. Compute Requirements Estimate
- Training NaViL‑2B on 500M pairs with max 4096 tokens per image + text, global batch 7k, for 70k steps requires substantial compute (several hundred GPU‑days on A100). Scaling‑law experiments will need careful sub‑sampling to fit budget.
- We will start with smaller proxy experiments to validate architecture, then scale up.

### 11. Final Deliverable
The plan above provides a thorough guide to implement the NaViL framework, run all reported experiments, and evaluate the model. For unclear aspects, we will adopt reasonable defaults from related work and be ready to adjust based on empirical checks. The next step is to translate this plan into modular Python code (model modules, data pipelines, training loops, evaluation scripts).

# for the three training stages (S1.1, S1.2, S2) of NaViL. It provides a utility

# Design assumptions:
# - The NaViL model's named parameters follow a naming convention that indicates
#   whether they belong to the visual or linguistic modality. The MoELLM module,
#   when extending the base LLM with modality-specific experts, must rename all
#   textual (linguistic) parameters to contain the substring "linguistic".
#   Similarly, visual expert parameters contain "visual". Non-expert parts of the
#   LLM (e.g., token embeddings, final layer norm, lm_head) are considered linguistic
#   and must also contain "linguistic" in their names for correct freezing.
# - Visual encoder and connector parameters do NOT contain "linguistic".
# - The freeze_pattern from the stage configuration is a list of substrings;
#   parameters whose name includes ANY of these substrings will be frozen (requires_grad=False).
# - At the beginning of each stage, ALL parameters are first set to trainable
#   (requires_grad=True) before applying the new pattern, ensuring that parameters
#   previously frozen (e.g., linguistic attention in S1.1) become trainable again
#   if the pattern changes (e.g., S1.2 unfreezes attention).

# Mapping of stages to freeze patterns (from config.yaml):
#   S1.1: freeze_pattern = ["linguistic"]
#         → All parameters with "linguistic" in their name are frozen.
#         This includes the entire linguistic MoE (attention & FFN) and the base
#         LLM’s embedding, norm, and head layers (if named accordingly).
#         Visual encoder, connector, and visual MoE experts remain trainable.
#
#   S1.2: freeze_pattern = ["linguistic.ffn"]
#         → Only linguistic FFN parameters are frozen (the linguistic attention
#         parameters are unfrozen). This matches the paper’s description:
#         “the textual parameters within the self-attention layers are also unfrozen”.
#         Note: we assume that linguistic attention parameters have names like
#         "*linguistic.attention*" (not "linguistic.ffn"), so they are not matched.
#
#   S2:   freeze_pattern = []
#         → No parameters are frozen; the entire model is trainable.

# Implementation details for `apply_freeze_pattern`:
#   1. Accept a torch.nn.Module and a list of string patterns (may be empty).
#   2. Iterate over all named parameters of the model (model.named_parameters()).
#      - First, set requires_grad = True for every parameter (reset).
#   3. If the pattern list is not empty, for each parameter, check whether its
#      name contains any of the patterns. If yes, set requires_grad = False.
#   4. Log the number of trainable vs frozen parameters for verification.
#
# Edge cases:
# - Patterns may match partially; we use simple substring containment. There is
#   no need for regex, as the config patterns are simple substrings ("linguistic",
#   "linguistic.ffn"). The dot in "linguistic.ffn" is part of the string.
# - Parameters of the visual encoder/connector typically have names like
#   "visual_encoder.layers.0...." or "connector.mlp.0.weight". These do not contain
#   "linguistic", so they remain trainable in all stages.
# - If the naming convention is not fully adhered to (e.g., some base LLM layer
#   does not contain "linguistic"), it would incorrectly stay trainable. This is
#   an implementation contract for the MoELLM module: it must rename or wrap the
#   linguistic parts such that they carry the "linguistic" substring.
#
# The Trainer will call this function at the beginning of each stage before
# creating the optimizer, ensuring that only the intended subset of parameters
# receives gradients.

# Function signature and pseudocode:
def apply_freeze_pattern(model: nn.Module, freeze_pattern: List[str]) -> None:
    """
    Reset all parameters to trainable, then freeze those whose name contains any
    of the substrings in freeze_pattern.
    """
    # Step 1: Unfreeze everything
    for param in model.parameters():
        param.requires_grad = True

    # Step 2: Apply freeze patterns
    if freeze_pattern:
        frozen_count = 0
        for name, param in model.named_parameters():
            if any(pattern in name for pattern in freeze_pattern):
                param.requires_grad = False
                frozen_count += 1
        trainable_count = sum(p.requires_grad for p in model.parameters())
        print(f"[Stages] Freeze pattern applied: {freeze_pattern}. "
              f"Trainable params: {trainable_count}, frozen: {frozen_count}.")
    else:
        print("[Stages] No freeze pattern – all parameters are trainable.")

# Additional helper: function to retrieve trainable parameters for optimizer.
def get_trainable_params(model: nn.Module) -> list:
    return [p for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad]
